prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff ERISA participant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plan administrator's decision is arbitrary and capricious when it relies on a file-only review and disregards treating physicians without explanation.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Administrator's Denial Was Arbitrary and Capricious Because It Rested on a Paper Review and Rejected the Treating Physicians' Opinions Without Explanation.**

Review under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard is deferential. It is not toothless. *McDonald v. W.-S. Life Ins. Co.*, 347 F.3d 161, 172 (6th Cir. 2003), explains that the standard does not reduce judicial review to a rubber stamp of the administrator's decision. A decision survives only if it is the result of a deliberate, principled reasoning process and is supported by substantial evidence. *Id.* at 169. *Evans v. UnumProvident Corp.*, 434 F.3d 866, 876 (6th Cir. 2006), applies the same test. The decision here fails that test for two related reasons.

**A. The Administrator Disregarded the Treating Physicians Without Explanation.**

An administrator need not give treating physicians special deference. *Black & Decker Disability Plan v. Nord*, 538 U.S. 822, 834 (2003). But it "may not arbitrarily refuse to credit a claimant's reliable evidence, including the opinions of a treating physician." *Id.* The Sixth Circuit enforces that limit. A plan may not reject a treating physician's opinion summarily. It must give reasons for adopting a contrary view. *Elliott v. Metro. Life Ins. Co.*, 473 F.3d 613, 620 (6th Cir. 2006); *Evans*, 434 F.3d at 877. In *Kalish v. Liberty Mutual/Liberty Life Assurance Co. of Boston*, 419 F.3d 501, 508 (6th Cir. 2005), the court held a denial arbitrary where the administrator did not engage with the claimant's medical evidence. *Smith v. Continental Casualty Co.*, 450 F.3d 253, 263–64 (6th Cir. 2006), and *Javery v. Lucent Technologies, Inc. Long Term Disability Plan for Management or LBA Employees*, 741 F.3d 686, 700–01 (6th Cir. 2014), likewise reject denials that did not meaningfully address the opinions of the claimant's own doctors.

Here, Plaintiff's treating physicians examined her over time. They documented her objective findings and limitations and concluded she could not work. The denial letters do not say why those conclusions were wrong. They do not identify contrary clinical findings. They do not say the treating physicians' observations were unreliable. They simply adopt the contrary conclusion of a reviewer who never met Plaintiff. That is the unexplained rejection *Elliott* and *Evans* forbid. A decision that does not show why the administrator preferred one medical view over another is not the product of a "deliberate, principled reasoning process." *McDonald*, 347 F.3d at 169.

**B. Reliance on a File-Only Review Compounds the Error.**

A file review is not improper in itself. But the Sixth Circuit has recognized that failing to examine the claimant "may, in some cases, raise questions about the thoroughness and accuracy of the benefits determination." *Calvert v. Firstar Fin., Inc.*, 409 F.3d 286, 295 (6th Cir. 2005). The concern is greatest when the administrator pairs a file review with a rejection of the examining physicians' conclusions. *Id.* at 296–97; *Kalish*, 419 F.3d at 508. The concern is also greatest when the reviewer's opinion rests on the absence of objective evidence for a condition that the treating physicians' own examinations documented. *See Elliott*, 473 F.3d at 621; *Smith*, 450 F.3d at 263–64.

The administrator here relied on the paper review of a non-examining consultant. It did not order an independent medical examination, though the plan allowed one. It also did not explain why the treating physicians' firsthand findings carried less weight than the consultant's reading of the same records.

**C. The Administrator's Structural Conflict of Interest Heightens the Scrutiny.**

The administrator both decides claims and pays benefits from its own funds. That dual role is a conflict of interest, and courts weigh it when reviewing the decision. *Moon v. Unum Provident Corp.*, 405 F.3d 373, 381–82 (6th Cir. 2005); *Bennett v. Kemper Nat'l Servs., Inc.*, 514 F.3d 547, 553–54 (6th Cir. 2008). A conflict matters most when other circumstances suggest it affected the outcome. A selective, one-sided evaluation of the medical record is one such circumstance. A file review that favors the payor, combined with an unexplained rejection of the treating physicians, is another. *See Calvert*, 409 F.3d at 295.

**D. Conclusion on the Merits.**

The administrator relied on a non-examining reviewer's paper assessment. It gave no reasoned basis for discounting the treating physicians. It operated under a structural conflict. Under *Elliott*, *Evans*, *Calvert*, and *Kalish*, those facts together make the denial arbitrary and capricious. The Court should reverse and direct an award of benefits. In the alternative, it should remand for a full and fair review that addresses the treating physicians' opinions.
